questions.q: What is the definition of a secondary theme in literature, and how does it differ from the primary theme?
questions.a: A secondary theme is a subordinate idea that supports, contrasts with, or adds complexity to the primary theme. The primary theme is the central, overarching message (here: the absurdity of class pride symbolised by moustaches); secondary themes are smaller, specific ideas (e.g., economic exploitation, performance of identity) that branch off from it. A wrong answer that equates secondary themes with subplots or minor characters reveals the student cannot distinguish between narrative structure and thematic architecture.

questions.q: In your own words, explain how the theme of "economic exploitation" functions as a secondary theme in the story, using Ramanand's character as evidence.
questions.a: Economic exploitation operates through Ramanand's dual role as grocer and moneylender: he profits from peasants' distress by buying wheat cheap and lending at high interest, then uses Khan Azam Khan's desperation to acquire heirlooms at a fraction of their value. The moustache dispute becomes a tool for asset stripping. A wrong answer that only describes Ramanand as "greedy" without linking his actions to the structural exploitation of the peasantry shows the student cannot abstract a systemic theme from character behaviour.

questions.q: Identify the exact moment in the text where the secondary theme of "commodification of honour" becomes explicit. Quote the relevant lines and explain how honour is treated as a transactional good.
questions.a: The moment is when Khan Azam Khan says: "Any price will do, so long as you bring the tip of your moustache down" (referring to the seven-generation necklace). Honour (the tiger moustache's exclusivity) is literally bought with ancestral gold. The moustache tip becomes a commodity with a price tag. A wrong answer that cites the nose-ring scene instead misses the escalation: the nose-ring was for survival; the necklace is *solely* for the moustache, proving honour has become a pure transaction.

questions.q: Analyse how the secondary theme of "the shift from feudal to commercial power" is embodied in the power dynamic between Khan Azam Khan and Ramanand. Use two contrasting details from their descriptions.
questions.a: Khan Azam Khan embodies decaying feudal power: "faded remnants of a gold-brocaded waistcoat," "hasn't even a patch of land left," but wears the tiger moustache of "noblemen and councillors." Ramanand embodies rising commercial power: "doing well out of the recent fall in the price of wheat," "built up his business on the maxim that the customer is always right," wears the goat moustache of the "commercial bourgeoisie." The feudal lord has symbols without substance; the merchant has substance without symbols — and wins. A wrong answer that sees them as equals in a petty fight misses the historical transition the story encodes.

questions.q: Evaluate the role of the village community (landlord, priest, peasants, elders) in the climax. Do they uphold justice or reinforce the absurd social order? Justify with two pieces of evidence.
questions.a: They reinforce the absurd order. Evidence 1: The landlord calls Ramanand's conditional surrender ("next time you come... I shall bring that tip down") "fair," legitimising the delay tactic. Evidence 2: The priest threatens excommunication *only* for breaking the moustache promise, not for exploiting a starving man. The community validates the symbolic code over human dignity. A wrong answer claiming they ensure a "fair deal" because a deed was signed shows the student cannot critically read the irony of the witnesses' complicity.

questions.q: Write a four-line dialogue set ten years after the story ends. Khan Azam Khan has lost his house; Ramanand owns it. The dialogue must reveal the secondary theme of "the complete triumph of commercial power over feudal pride."
questions.a:
Khan: "This courtyard heard seven generations of tiger moustaches."
Ramanand: "Now it hears the grind of my mill. The goat won, Khan."
Khan: "You wear the goat still?"
Ramanand: "I wear whatever sells. The Sultan's blood? I bought it cheap."
Criteria: Shows shifted ownership, references both moustache symbols, demonstrates Ramanand's cynical commodification of the very ancestry Khan died for. A poor answer merely repeats the original quarrel without showing historical change.
